summary:
This evaluation covered 7 chat-task evals (5 substantive content evals plus 2 negative-trigger evals) run 3 times each on an AWS Elemental MediaPackage/MediaConvert DRM/key-management domain.

Trigger firing: Both variants fired as expected in all evals where this was measured (3/3 in every eval), including the two negative-trigger evals, which were otherwise skipped for all other dimensions (expected_output, assertions, metrics, consistency) because they are "should_trigger: false" cases — this is expected skipping, not a performance gap.

Expected output / assertions: Across the five substantive evals, with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions at or near 100% in every case (high confidence throughout). without_skill's performance varied sharply by eval:
- In spk-rotation-limit, spk-sl3000-audio, spk-widevine-uuid, and spk-key-counts, without_skill failed the expected output entirely (0/3) and failed almost all assertions (e.g., 0/9, 1/9, 0/6, 1/9), with the pattern "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" on the core LLM-judged and regex assertions. A couple of individual regex checks (e.g., mentioning "v1" or "3") were flaky for without_skill (passing 1/3) rather than uniformly failing.
- In spk-cbcs-choice, without_skill was much closer to with_skill: it met expected output 2/3 vs with_skill's 3/3, and passed 5/6 vs 6/6 assertions. One assertion ("mentions 'cbcs'") passed for both variants in all runs — this assertion isn't discriminating between them. The core LLM-judged accuracy/completeness assertion was flaky for without_skill (2/3) while consistent for with_skill (3/3).
All expected-output and assertion judgments carried high (or in cbcs's LLM judgment, high) confidence, so these are not low-confidence findings.

Quality comparison: Head-to-head quality scoring was only possible for spk-cbcs-choice (2 of 3 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped); there, outcomes were close and mixed — with_skill favored on 3 criterion-counts, without_skill on 2, with 1 comparable, at medium confidence. For the other four substantive evals, all quality pairs were skipped (0 of 3 evaluated), so no direct quality comparison data exists there — this is an absence of data, not a negative mark for either variant.

Runtime and cost: Results were mixed and eval-dependent, not a consistent pattern favoring one variant. with_skill was slower/costlier in spk-sl3000-audio (11s/$0.10 vs without_skill's 4s/$0.04) and spk-widevine-uuid (5s/$0.05 vs 0s/$0.00), while without_skill was slower/costlier in spk-rotation-limit (9s/$0.08 vs with_skill's 4s/$0.04) and spk-cbcs-choice (10s/$0.09 vs 4s/$0.04). In spk-key-counts, runtime and cost were essentially equal (3s/$0.03 each). No runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold where measured.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score ~2.67) in all five substantive evals. without_skill was also "mostly_consistent" (~2.33) in three evals, but dropped to "inconsistent" (score 1.67) in spk-cbcs-choice and spk-key-counts — the same two evals where without_skill also showed flaky assertion/expected-output behavior, suggesting without_skill's run-to-run variability may be linked to its weaker or inconsistent content accuracy in those cases.

Overall pattern: On the dimensions with the clearest, highest-confidence signal (expected output match and assertion pass rates), with_skill was consistently strong across all five substantive evals, while without_skill ranged from failing nearly all checks (four evals) to performing close to with_skill with some flakiness (one eval, spk-cbcs-choice, where direct quality scoring was mixed/close and one assertion passed for both). Runtime/cost tradeoffs ran in both directions depending on the eval and do not show a systematic pattern favoring either variant. Direct quality-score comparisons were only available for one eval and were mixed at medium confidence; for the rest, this dimension is simply missing data rather than evidence of parity or difference.

spk-rotation-limit.summary:
This eval tested a chat scenario about AWS Elemental MediaPackage SPEKE v2 key rotation behavior, run 3 times for each variant. The trigger behavior fired in all cases (3/3), confirming the scenario under test was properly exercised.

On the core measure, expected output, the two variants diverge sharply: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%) with high confidence, while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%), also with high confidence judgments (so this is not a low-confidence artifact — the judgments themselves are reliable, even though the gap is stark).

This divergence is echoed in the per-assertion data (9 total assertion checks per variant):
- with_skill passed 9/9 (100%); without_skill passed 1/9 (11%).
- Two assertions show a clean "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern: one LLM-judged assertion about correctly describing SPEKE v2 disabling rotation, UnprocessableEntityException behavior, and the v1 requirement (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 0/3, both high confidence); and one regex check for the literal string "UnprocessableEntityException" (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 0/3).
- A third assertion (regex check for "v1") was flaky for without_skill (1/3 passing) while with_skill passed consistently (3/3). This indicates some run-to-run variability in without_skill's wording even on a simple surface-level check, beyond the deeper content gap.
- No assertion passed for neither variant, and none passed only for without_skill — all assertion-level differences favor with_skill in this instance.

On quality comparison, no pairwise quality judgments could actually be made (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no quality-comparison data to weigh here — this dimension is simply absent, not a wash or a tie.

On output consistency across repeated runs, both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall, with with_skill scoring slightly higher (2.67 vs 2.33) and showing 2 "consistent" dimensions vs 1 for without_skill (which had 2 "mostly_consistent" and 1 "consistent"). Both are rated with high average confidence, and the difference is modest.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was faster (4s vs 9s) and cheaper ($0.04 vs $0.08) than without_skill, with essentially identical context-window utilization (~4.4–4.5%) and no compaction events for either.

Overall picture: this is not a case of balanced tradeoffs — with_skill met the expected output and nearly all assertions consistently across runs, while without_skill failed the expected-output check in every run and the majority of assertions, including one clear content-accuracy assertion and one exact-string assertion. Variant_b was also faster and cheaper in this instance, and slightly more consistent across repeated runs, with quality-comparison data unavailable to add further nuance. All underlying judgments reported here were made with high confidence, lending weight to these findings, though this is based on only 3 repetitions per variant for a single eval/task.

Trigger behavior fired in all 3/3 runs, confirming the test scenario was exercised as intended for both variants.

On expected output, there is a clear and consistent difference: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%, high confidence). This is mirrored exactly in the assertion-level results — both assertions (the LLM-judged explanation about SL2000 downgrade/separate audio key, and the regex check for "SL2000") passed 6/6 for with_skill and failed 0/6 for without_skill. Both assertions show the identical pattern (with_skill passes, without_skill fails) across all three runs, so this isn't a case of one weak assertion dragging down an aggregate — the failure is consistent and corroborated by both an LLM-based and a simple regex-based check, and confidence is high throughout, so this finding is reasonably solid rather than a measurement artifact.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was notably faster (4s vs 11s) and cheaper ($0.04 vs $0.10) than with_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~4.4-4.6%), with no compaction needed for either.

Quality comparison data is not available: all 3 pairs were skipped, so no head-to-head quality judgment could be made between the two outputs beyond the expected-output/assertion checks.

Output consistency was similar for both variants, each rated "mostly_consistent" overall (with_skill scored 2.67, without_skill scored 2.33, both with high-confidence ratings), indicating neither variant showed major run-to-run instability, though with_skill was slightly more consistent across dimensions (2 consistent + 1 mostly-consistent vs. without_skill's 1 consistent + 2 mostly-consistent).

Overall, the dominant signal here is the expected-output/assertion failure for without_skill versus success for with_skill, which is consistent, high-confidence, and corroborated by two independent assertion types. This stands alongside a cost/speed advantage for without_skill and roughly comparable consistency for both, with no direct quality-comparison data available to weigh against the correctness gap.

spk-cbcs-choice.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat-based task (recommending the correct DRM/CMAF encryption scheme — "cbcs" — for FairPlay/CBC family support) with 3 runs per variant.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in all 3/3 runs, so the eval is fully applicable.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%), without_skill in 2/3 runs (67%). Both measurements are rated high-confidence, so this gap appears to be a real, reliably-judged difference rather than a measurement artifact, though it's based on only 3 runs per variant.

Assertions: with_skill passed all assertions (6/6, 100%); without_skill passed 5/6 (83%). Breaking this down, one assertion (a regex check for the literal mention of "cbcs") passed 100% of the time for both variants — this assertion doesn't discriminate between them. The other assertion (an LLM-judged check on whether the response correctly justifies the cbcs recommendation) was flaky for without_skill (2/3 pass) while passing consistently for with_skill (3/3), both at high judge confidence. This is the one assertion driving the overall gap, and it points to an occasional reasoning/justification lapse in without_skill rather than a wholesale failure.

Quality comparison: Only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for quality (1 skipped). Across those pairs, results were mixed and close: overall quality favored with_skill in 3 sub-comparisons and without_skill in 2, with 1 rated comparable, at medium confidence. Per-criterion, accuracy and completeness were split evenly (1-1) between the variants, while actionability leaned slightly toward with_skill (1 favoring with_skill, 1 comparable, 0 for without_skill). Given the small sample (2 pairs) and medium confidence, this should be read as inconclusive/roughly even rather than a clear preference.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran notably faster (~4s avg) and cheaper (~$0.04) than without_skill (~10s avg, ~$0.09). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the 2 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was nearly identical (~4.3-4.4%) with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was "mostly consistent" (score 2.67/3, 2 consistent + 1 mostly-consistent dimension, high confidence). without_skill was "inconsistent" (score 1.67/3, 2 mostly-consistent + 1 inconsistent dimension, medium confidence). This aligns with the flaky assertion result above — without_skill's output varied more across runs on this task.

Overall picture: with_skill met the expected output and assertions more reliably and showed more run-to-run consistency, while also being faster and cheaper on this small sample. without_skill's quality was comparable to with_skill on the (limited, medium-confidence) quality comparison, but it showed more variability in reasoning/justification across repeated runs and took longer and cost more. These findings rest on a small number of runs (3 total, with only 2 quality pairs evaluated), so while the directional differences are consistent across several dimensions, the overall confidence in the magnitude of the gap is moderate.

overall.summary: with_skill wins overall (3 vs 2 criterion wins out of 6 judgments, avg confidence: medium).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs arrive at the same correct final recommendation (cbcs), and the core technical reasoning is largely accurate in both. However, Output A makes a claim that is technically incorrect/misleading: it states 'cenc and cbc1 are AES-CTR/CBC full-sample, and cens is CTR-based partial' — mixing up scheme names (cenc is CTR full-sample, cbc1 is CBC full-sample, cens is CTR partial, cbcs is CBC partial), and asserts these would 'break Apple device playback' without acknowledging that cenc is actually usable by Widevine/PlayReady, just not FairPlay. Output B explicitly and correctly notes that Widevine and PlayReady are compatible with either cbcs or cenc, which is a more nuanced and accurate characterization of the DRM compatibility matrix. More importantly, Output B is honest about not having an actual 'skill' resource for this, correctly identifying that the agent's skill catalog does not cover this domain, and clearly labels its answer as general reference knowledge rather than a skill-sourced answer. This transparency about the information source is a significant accuracy/honesty consideration, since the user explicitly asked 'does the skill recommend' — Output A answers as if a skill said this without any indication of whether it actually consulted a skill, which could be seen as fabricating or misattributing the source of the recommendation.

Output B: 'I checked, and there's no skill in this agent space that addresses CMAF DRM encryption scheme selection... For general reference (not sourced from any skill): ... FairPlay only supports `cbcs` while Widevine and PlayReady are compatible with either `cbcs` or `cenc`.'

Output B also provides the same actionable recommendation but frames it as unverified general reference and offers to verify against documentation, which is slightly less confident/actionable as a final answer, though it does still give the same practical guidance and offers a concrete next step (verification).

Output B: 'For general reference (not sourced from any skill): AWS MediaPackage documentation typically recommends `cbcs`... If you'd like, I can verify this directly against current AWS MediaPackage documentation.'

criteria.reasoning: Output B is more complete in addressing the actual question asked, which specifically references 'the skill' — Output B investigates and reports on whether such a skill exists before providing the fallback general answer, fully addressing the premise of the question. Output A ignores the 'skill' framing entirely and just asserts the answer as if from a skill, which is incomplete with respect to the user's actual query about skill-based guidance. Output B also covers the cenc compatibility nuance for Widevine/PlayReady that Output A omits (and gets wrong elsewhere), making it more complete on the DRM compatibility details.

Output A never addresses whether a 'skill' was actually consulted.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly identify CBCS as the answer, which aligns with known AWS MediaPackage/CPIX documentation that FairPlay requires CBCS (AES-CBC pattern) encryption while Widevine and PlayReady can work with either CENC or CBCS. Output A introduces a claim that CENC supports 'Irdeto' as a DRM system, which is not a standard characterization in MediaPackage/CPIX documentation — Irdeto is typically a DRM provider/vendor, not listed alongside PlayReady/Widevine/FairPlay as a 'DRM system' in this context, and this specific claim appears to be an inaccuracy or fabrication. Output B's explanation is more technically grounded, correctly describing the CENC specification's four scheme values (cenc, cbc1, cbcs, cens) with accurate characterizations of each (AES-CTR vs AES-CBC, full-sample vs pattern encryption) which matches the ISO/IEC 23001-7 CENC spec accurately. Output A's claim about CENC including Irdeto is suspect and not well substantiated, making Output B more likely accurate in its supporting details.

Both outputs directly answer the question with a clear, actionable recommendation (use CBCS) and explain why in a way that would let a user make an informed decision. Neither provides step-by-step configuration instructions, but the question was more conceptual/advisory in nature ('which scheme and why') rather than asking for implementation steps. Both are equally actionable in the sense of giving a clear decision and rationale that could guide a user's configuration choice in MediaPackage or CPIX.

spk-key-counts.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-based task involving AWS Elemental MediaPackage/MediaConvert key counting (resolution-tier video keys plus audio keys, and the '8 keys' preset-numbering ambiguity). The trigger condition for the test fired in all 3 runs, so the behavior under test was exercised as intended.

On meeting the expected output, with_skill passed all 3 runs (100%) with high-confidence judgments, while without_skill failed all 3 runs (0%), also with high-confidence judgments — so this is a clear, high-confidence divergence rather than a borderline or noisy call.

At the assertion level, with_skill passed 9/9 individual assertion checks (100%) and without_skill passed only 1/9 (11%). Breaking this down by assertion:
- The core content assertion (correct key counts and warning about the '8 keys' shorthand) passed for with_skill in all 3 runs and failed for without_skill in all 3 runs — a clean split where one variant consistently satisfies the requirement and the other consistently does not.
- A simple regex check for the presence of '5' passed for with_skill in all 3 runs but failed for without_skill in all 3 runs.
- A regex check for the presence of '3' passed for with_skill in all 3 runs, but was flaky for without_skill (passed only 1 of 3 runs), indicating some run-to-run variability in without_skill's output beyond the clear accuracy gap.

No assertions passed for neither variant, and none passed for both — every assertion showed at least a partial difference favoring with_skill.

On runtime and cost, the two variants were essentially identical: both averaged ~3 seconds and ~$0.03 per run, with very low and similar context-window utilization (4.4% vs 3.9%) and no compaction events for either. So there is no meaningful efficiency tradeoff distinguishing the two here.

The quality comparison component could not be evaluated: all 3 pairs were skipped, with zero pairs actually compared. This means no head-to-head quality judgment is available to weigh against the other findings — it's absent data, not a sign of weakness for either variant.

Output consistency (stability across repeated runs) differed: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, with 2 of 3 dimensions fully consistent), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.67, with 1 of 3 dimensions inconsistent), both at high judgment confidence. This aligns with the flakiness seen in the '3' assertion for without_skill.

Overall, across the dimensions that could be measured — expected-output success, per-assertion pass rates, and output consistency — with_skill showed uniformly stronger and more stable results than without_skill on this single task, with high confidence in those judgments. Cost and runtime were equivalent between the two, and no comparative quality-judgment data was available to add further nuance. Because this reflects only one eval task (three repeated runs), the generalizability of this pattern to other tasks is not established by this data alone.
